statements: Rates here are measured over the 2,533 denials the payer has already answered, out of 5,398 denials in this population.
212 denials have been resubmitted and are still waiting on the payer. They are counted in neither the wins nor the losses.
2,653 denials have no resubmission on file. Some of those have not been worked yet rather than never; nothing in the data separates the two.
Everything above is as the data stood on Aug 2, 2026.

How often denials are worked is read only over denials old enough that a resubmission would have gone out by now: clinical / medical necessity 73 days, coding 18 days, final — non-appealable 95 days, registration and eligibility 26 days, routing and coordination of benefits 44 days. That waiting period does not apply to the recovery rate itself. A recovery rate is measured only over denials the payer has already answered, so a denial that is too recent to have an answer is simply not in it — there is nothing to exclude, and nothing is.

findings.title: What the open denials are worth
findings.statement: Working the 2,865 open denials still outstanding ($5,749,495.12 denied) should bring back about $309,129.94, somewhere between $224,079.89 and $436,678.86. That figure is built one population at a time: its open dollars are split by whether the filing deadline has passed, each side is priced at the rate denials on that side actually come back at — 44.2% for what is still inside the deadline (over 2,454 answered denials) and 3.8% for what is past it (over 79 answered denials) — and the result is multiplied by 44.5 cents on the dollar, which is what a win has actually returned across 1,087 recovered denials. Priced by payer and denial type: each population's open denials at that population's own measured rate.

findings.title: The gap between your strongest and weakest payer
findings.statement: Northbridge Commercial gives back 56.8% of what you resubmit (over 148 answered denials); Lakewood Medicaid MCO gives back 29.1% (over 117 answered denials). That is a gap of 27.7 percentage points. The chance of seeing a gap this size if the two were really the same is under 1 in 1,000. The gap itself is somewhere between 15.8 percentage points and 38.4 percentage points.

findings.title: The gap between your strongest and weakest denial type
findings.statement: Coding gives back 62.2% of what you resubmit (over 508 answered denials); final — non-appealable gives back 3.0% (over 66 answered denials). That is a gap of 59.2 percentage points. The chance of seeing a gap this size if the two were really the same is under 1 in 1,000. The gap itself is somewhere between 50.7 percentage points and 63.8 percentage points.

findings.title: What waiting costs
findings.statement: Denials resubmitted within 0-14 days come back 54.4% of the time. Once the wait reaches 61+ days it is 14.2%.

context_notes: These rates are measured on denials that were worked and then answered, and they are being applied to denials that have not been worked. Those are not the same mix: clinical / medical necessity and final — non-appealable — the kinds that come back least often — are 61.0% of the open denied dollars but only 23.5% of the answered denials the rates come from. Pricing each kind of denial at its own rate is what keeps that from inflating the total, which is why the money above is cut that way.

A win is not the full denied amount. Across the 1,087 denials that came back, payers allowed $1,234,436.05 of $2,773,981.37 denied — 44.5 cents on the dollar. Every figure above is multiplied by that.

How often denials are worked is read only over denials old enough that a resubmission would have gone out by now: clinical / medical necessity 73 days, coding 18 days, final — non-appealable 95 days, registration and eligibility 26 days, routing and coordination of benefits 44 days. Younger denials are left out rather than counted as unworked. You can change these anytime.

Getting the work out inside 0-14 days is worth 40.1 percentage points on the recovery rate compared with the slowest group. That is not all speed: the slowest group also holds the kinds of denial that come back least often, so read it as the most speed could be worth rather than what it is worth.
Clinical / medical necessity denials currently take a median of 31 days to go back out.
Coding denials currently take a median of 9 days to go back out.
Final — non-appealable denials currently take a median of 49 days to go back out.
Registration and eligibility denials currently take a median of 13 days to go back out.
Routing and coordination of benefits denials currently take a median of 20 days to go back out.
The drop is steeper where the filing limit is confirmed than where it is still a planning default, so the two are shown apart. Treating every limit as confirmed overstates the cliff.
None of the 39 answered denials filed past a confirmed deadline came back. That is not the same as never: on this many denials the true rate could still be as high as 9.0%.
Clinical denials rest on medical necessity and need documentation, not a correction — they are worked more slowly and won less often.
Coding denials are usually correctable — a modifier, a code pair, or a unit count that can be fixed and sent back.
Registration and eligibility denials usually trace to demographics or coverage captured at the front end, and are correctable once the right coverage is found.
Routing and COB denials usually mean the claim went to the wrong payer or in the wrong order; the fix is a rebill to the right one.
